equation_request.abstract: In recent years, deep learning has had a profound impact on machine learning and artificial intelligence. At the same time, algorithms for quantum computers have been shown to efficiently solve some problems that are intractable on conventional, classical computers. We show that quantum computing not only reduces the time required to train a deep restricted Boltzmann machine, but also provides a richer and more comprehensive framework for deep learning than classical computing and leads to significant improvements in the optimization of the underlying objective function. Our quantum methods also permit efficient training of full Boltzmann machines and multi–layer, fully connected models and do not have well known classical counterparts.

specification.problem: Training of (restricted) Boltzmann machines by maximizing the log-likelihood, where quantum methods are claimed to reduce training time and improve optimization. The abstract gives no explicit equations, so only the standard classical objective and gradient are reconstructed as background.
specification.reconstruction_scope: Smallest useful construction: a tiny RBM (e.g. 2 visible, 2 hidden units) with the standard energy function, Gibbs distribution, log-likelihood and gradient, plus a quantum-state encoding of the Gibbs distribution as a labelled assumption. The paper's actual quantum training algorithm, its state preparation, gradient estimation and the full Boltzmann machine and multi-layer extensions are outside this scope.

symbols.meaning: average log-likelihood objective over training data
Gibbs distribution encoded as a quantum state

equations.label: RBM energy
equations.latex: E(v,h) = -\sum_i b_i v_i - \sum_j d_j h_j - \sum_{i,j} v_i W_{ij} h_j
equations.description: Energy function of a restricted Boltzmann machine.
equations.justification: The abstract names the RBM but gives no equation; this is the standard form.

equations.label: Gibbs distribution
equations.description: Joint probability of the model; the marginal is P(v)=sum_h P(v,h).

equations.label: Log-likelihood objective
equations.description: Objective function to be maximized in training.
equations.justification: The abstract mentions optimizing the underlying objective function without specifying it; maximum likelihood is the standard choice.

equations.label: Weight gradient
equations.latex: \frac{\partial O_{ML}}{\partial W_{ij}}=\langle v_i h_j\rangle_{\text{data}}-\langle v_i h_j\rangle_{\text{model}}
equations.description: Gradient as the difference between data and model correlations; the model term is the costly part that quantum sampling would target.
assumptions: Data expectation is taken with clamped visible units

equations.label: Gibbs state encoding
equations.description: A coherent encoding of the model distribution; measuring in the computational basis samples from P.
equations.justification: Proposed construction for sampling the model term. The abstract does not state how the paper prepares states.
assumptions: Preparation of this state is available; its method is not specified

steps.description: Define the tiny RBM energy and Gibbs distribution.
Define the log-likelihood objective and its gradient.
Assumed: prepare the Gibbs-state encoding and sample it to estimate the model correlations in the gradient.

specification.measurement: Assumed: computational-basis measurement of both registers to sample (v,h) from P, estimating the model expectation.
specification.classical_postprocessing: Assumed: average samples to estimate the correlations, form the gradient and update W, b, d by gradient ascent.
assumptions: Binary RBM with 2 visible and 2 hidden units as the tiny instance
The quantum algorithm itself is not specified in the abstract; eq_5 is a placeholder construction
